transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-09 16:00 PDT
Length: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Noah Patel (Redwood SE), Sasha Reed (Peregrine CTO), Jamal Ortiz (Lead ML Eng), Rita Kapoor (Procurement)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on unit economics for Peregrine's planned LLM features. Peregrine has a constrained budget for inference, wants to understand hosted per-token pricing and levers (batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization, reserved capacity) vs dedicated/private options for latency-sensitive use cases. They requested benchmarks on their prompt set and compliance docs. Next steps include pricing sheet, benchmark run, and a technical deep dive on caching/quantization.

Topics: pricing, batching, KV/prefix cache, dedicated vs hosted, private/VPC, security (SOC2/KMS), timeline, procurement questions.

Transcript:
00:00 - Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros, we're from Redwood Inference, I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this deal, and Noah is our SE.
00:06 - Sasha: Hi, Sasha Reed, CTO at Peregrine. Jamal and Rita with me.
00:11 - Jamal: Jamal here.
00:12 - Rita: Rita, procurement.
00:14 - Maya: Cool. High level, Sasha, can you share the use case and where you are in validation?
00:20 - Sasha: Yeah, so we're building a real-time summarization and scoring feature for analyst notes. Target 100ms-ish tail latency for user-facing snippets, bulk batch jobs for nightly scoring is fine if slower. Budget is tight, we have an initial monthly cap of about 12k USD for inference, but willing to trade latency for cost if necessary. We're evaluating hosted and dedicated, maybe private for compliance.
00:45 - Noah: Got it. When you say 100ms tail, is that p95 or p99? And what's the typical sequence length?
00:51 - Sasha: We care about p95. Average input is 250 tokens, output about 80 tokens. Peak concurrent users around 40 in region, but spikes to 150 qps during morning digest.
01:05 - Maya: Good. So main axes: latency, cost, and compliance. We'll talk about the levers that move cost per token down: batching, prefix/KV cache, and quantization. Also the hosting model — hosted API versus Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity or Redwood Private — affects both unit cost and latency predictability.
01:22 - Jamal: Quick question: our models are mostly open weights we fine-tuned. Can you run hosted on our fine-tuned checkpoints or do we need private?
01:29 - Noah: You can do both. For hosted we support model onboarding for many open weights; there's a vetting process. If you need on-prem security or VPC-only, Private is better. Dedicated sits in between: reserved GPUs for your workload but managed by Redwood, gives stronger isolation and lower per-token cost via utilization.
01:45 - Rita: From procurement perspective, pricing clarity matters. We want to see committed pricing for reserved capacity and per-token for hosted, plus any overage rules.
01:52 - Maya: Absolutely. We'll send a commercial outline. For hosted, our standard is per-input-token + per-output-token pricing tiers, with volume discounts. For Dedicated, it's a monthly reserved capacity with included throughput and committed units; effective per-token drops as you utilize reserved pool and use batching.
02:08 - Sasha: Can you quantify the per-token difference? Ballpark numbers are fine.
02:12 - Noah: For a representative open decoder model at 8k context, on hosted at low-volume, you'd see something like $0.0008 per input token and $0.0012 per output token — that's illustrative. With Dedicated reserved capacity and good batching, your effective unit cost can fall 40-60%. But exact depends on sequence lengths, batching headroom, and cache hit rates.
02:35 - Jamal: That seems wide. Can you explain caching impact? We often see repeated prefixes — client metadata + previous summary.
02:41 - Noah: Sure. Prefix or KV cache stores the key/value past key states so we avoid recomputing early layers for repeated tokens. If a request reuses a prefix, we can hit the cache and only generate the tail tokens. Practically, if 30% of your tokens are cached across requests, you see near-linear reduction in decode compute and cost for those positions. But cache hit rate depends on how static the prefix is and session stickiness.
03:03 - Sasha: So for our 250 token input with 80 token output, if 70 tokens are cached we only pay for the rest?
03:10 - Noah: In effect, yes for compute; but networking and request overhead remain. Also, caching is more effective on dedicated/private where we can keep warm state and affinity. Hosted supports caching too but with some TTLs and cross-tenant limits.
03:23 - Rita: Any impacts on latency? Caching should help latency right?
03:26 - Noah: Generally yes — cache means less compute per request and lower latency, but it also introduces routing affinity (you want same node to hit cache). Dedicated gives stronger latency SLOs because of fixed capacity and affinity.
03:37 - Sasha: We also care about batch versus single-shot. Users expect interactivity. Can batching be used without hurting p95?
03:44 - Noah: Redwood runtime uses continuous batching with latency-aware policies. We can set max batching window like 8-12 ms for interactive tiers; small windows give limited batching gains but preserve p95. For non-interactive endpoints you can increase window to get larger gains. In practice for p95=100ms you can still get modest batching benefits if your workload has microbursts.
04:05 - Jamal: Any guardrails for tokenization differences? We saw one provider quoting tokens differently which messed our forecasting.
:04:12 - Maya: Good point. We align token accounting with byte-pair tokenizers commonly used and provide tokenized charge reports per request so you can forecast accurately. We'll share sample tokenization on your prompt set as part of the benchmark.
04:26 - Sasha: About quantization — you mentioned that as a lever. How safe is it for our fine-tuned models?
04:31 - Noah: Quantization reduces model memory and improves throughput, lowering cost. For many workloads 4-bit or 8-bit quantization preserves quality; there can be regressions, so we recommend running your evals. For high-sensitivity outputs we suggest validating on your prompt set; Noah can run A/B on Redwood Dedicated and surface quality deltas.
04:52 - Rita: On compliance, can you do SOC2? We need to see logs, KMS, and contractual terms.
04:58 - Maya: Yes. Redwood is SOC2 Type II (we'll share the cert). For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and all audit logs live in your control plane. For Dedicated we provide audited access logs and optional VPC peering. I'll attach our compliance pack link: https://rwd.co/compliance-pack and the SOC2 cert.
05:18 - Jamal: Network egress and data residency — if we use hosted in us-west, do you replicate in other regions? We need to ensure data stays in-region.
05:25 - Noah: Hosts are region-specific. Hosted API requests in us-west stay there unless you opt into cross-region features. Private/on-prem removes that concern.
05:31 - Sasha: Procurement question: reserve commitment length — monthly or annual? Early on we want month-to-month but may move to annual with discounts.
05:39 - Rita: Yep. Show us a path that starts with small month-to-month reserved slab.
05:43 - Maya: We can propose monthly reserved tiers and show the delta to annual. Also, we can structure pilot credits against future committed spend so risk is lower.
05:52 - Jamal: For the benchmark run, could you simulate our morning spike of 150 qps? That spike is when latency must hold.
05:59 - Noah: We'll simulate realistic qps and synthetic concurrency. If you provide sample prompts and expected concurrency curve, we can run both hosted and dedicated sims and report p50/p95/p99 and tokens/second and cost per 1k requests.
06:13 - Sasha: Sounds good. Also, curious about fallback policies — if dedicated capacity is saturated do you auto-failover to hosted?
06:20 - Noah: Yes, we support smart routing and fallback policies. You can configure primary dedicated with hosted fallback; the routing considers latency SLOs and cost. We also do model variant fallback — e.g., if a high-performance variant is out of capacity we can route to a slightly quantized or smaller model to preserve availability.
06:36 - Rita: Any hidden fees? Storage for KV cache? Logging retention?
06:40 - Maya: We'll include all line items. KV cache storage is usually included in dedicated plans; long-term snapshot retention and extended log retention are add-ons. We'll be explicit in the commercial outline.
06:51 - Sasha: If we go private later, how painful is migration from hosted/dedicated?
06:56 - Noah: We design the API and rollout tooling to make migrations smoother. You can pin model versions and rollout policies, and our console supports canary and A/B rollouts. For private we replicate model artifacts but the migration effort depends on whether you need air-gapped installs.
07:10 - Jamal: One more technical: how do you measure and bill for tokens with caching? Do you charge on raw token generation or net compute?
07:16 - Noah: We provide a tokenization view per request; billing aligns with compute performed. If cache avoids recomputation of N tokens, you'll see reduced compute-based billing for those tokens. We show both logical tokens and billed tokens on the report so you can reconcile.
07:29 - Sasha: Great. For the pilot, our success metrics: cost per 1k requests under 35 USD with p95 under 120ms and SOC2 evidence. If we hit that, procurement moves fast.
07:41 - Rita: Timeline — we need commercial by next Friday and a pilot benchmark within two weeks.
07:46 - Maya: We'll aim to deliver the commercial outline by 2025-07-11 and schedule the benchmark for the week after.
07:52 - Jamal: Anything else — tooling, SDKs? We integrate with Python and JS.
07:56 - Noah: We have SDKs for Python and JS, plus a Postman collection and a benchmark harness. We'll share a quickstart repo link and the bench harness we use internally.
08:07 - Sasha: Perfect. Thanks.
08:09 - Maya: Quick recap: Maya sends commercial outline + compliance links, Noah runs benchmark simulation with Peregrine prompts, Sasha shares prompt corpus and concurrency curve, schedule SE deep-dive. Anything to add?
08:20 - Rita: No, that's all.
08:22 - Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with attachments.

End of transcript.
